video_title: Is THORChain Centralized Enough to Stop North Korea From Laundering Stolen Crypto?
gist: A heated debate between security researcher Taylor Monaghan and ThorChain co-founder Chad over whether ThorChain can and should halt DPRK laundering routes: Taylor argues routes that are 90-100% stolen funds could be paused with existing halt/pause functions (as was done for ThorChain's own incidents), while Chad insists 2/3 node consensus takes days-to-weeks, the protocol is more decentralized than Bitcoin/Ethereum, and only centralizing redesign could enable censorship. Key investor-relevant threads: concentrated node operator set (4 operators run 39 nodes), closed-source TSS library, money-transmission custody/control legal risk, TRM flagging ThorChain outflows, and fee spikes tied to hack-driven volume (transcript is a garbled auto-translation; hack names are mangled).

themes.theme: Can ThorChain technically block DPRK flows

insights.claim: ThorChain's co-founder says the protocol has no code to censor individual transactions or wallets, and any action needs a two-thirds node consensus that takes about three days on average and up to two weeks, making per-transaction blocking ineffective.
insights.speaker: Chad (ThorChain co-founder)
insights.so_what: ThorChain will not proactively stop hack-driven flows; expect continued laundering volume after major hacks and the reputational/regulatory overhang that comes with it.
insights.quote: it takes about three days on average, sometimes up to two weeks, to get a two- thirds majority consensus from the protocol

insights.claim: Taylor Monaghan argues that during a recent hack nearly 100% of assets on ThorChain's XRP-to-ETH route were directly stolen funds, so simply turning off that route would have pushed launderers elsewhere.
insights.speaker: Taylor Monaghan (security expert)
insights.so_what: Route-level volume concentration from a single illicit source is a measurable on-chain signal; spikes on unusual routes after hacks indicate laundering, not organic demand.
insights.quote: it was almost 100% of the assets on that route during that time period that were directly stolen funds

insights.claim: Chad counters that halting trading would require in-flight swaps to go through a recovery migration needing two-thirds consensus (one to two weeks), and address-level blocks would be defeated because attackers simply switch to new addresses.
insights.speaker: Chad (ThorChain co-founder)
insights.so_what: Any halt would freeze the protocol's main revenue source for weeks, which is why node operators are economically disinclined to act.
insights.quote: But the attacker would simply change the address, sending to any other arbitrary address, and continue trading.

insights.claim: Laura Shin points out ThorChain already has ETH-trading-halt and BTC-trading-halt functions, and that an ETH halt could have returned ETH and XRP swap funds to the sender during the hack.
insights.speaker: Laura Shin (host)
insights.so_what: The 'can't' framing is contested: existing chain-specific halt switches mean inaction is partly a choice, raising regulatory 'knowledge and control' exposure.
insights.quote: The ETH trading stop function could have returned ETH and XRP funds from swaps during the Bitcat hack to the sender.

insights.claim: A 'make pause' function lets any single ThorChain node pause all chains for 720 blocks (about an hour), a fast lever that was apparently not used during the recent DPRK flows.
insights.speaker: Laura Shin (host)
insights.so_what: A single node can unilaterally buy time, undermining the claim that response is necessarily slow; watch whether any node uses it during the next major hack.
insights.quote: allows any single node to pause all chains for 720 blocks, or about an hour

insights.claim: Laura Shin cites the DAO-hack precedent where ShapeShift played whack-a-mole with an apparently bot-driven hacker and, despite imperfect blocking, made laundering hard enough that the hacker gave up at points.
insights.speaker: Laura Shin (host)
insights.so_what: Partial friction measurably reduces laundering throughput; 'can't block everything' is not the same as 'blocking is useless'.

insights.claim: Taylor Monaghan's specific ask is not a full shutdown but action whenever a particular route is over 90% directly stolen funds.
insights.speaker: Taylor Monaghan (security expert)
insights.so_what: A concrete, route-threshold policy is the compromise to watch for in governance proposals; adoption would cut hack-driven fee spikes.
insights.quote: when a certain route is over 90% directly stolen funds, then we have to do something

insights.claim: Chad argues North Korea's real goal is to reach Bitcoin, using ThorChain as the on-ramp, and that Bitcoin miners and Ethereum validators face the same consensus-based ability to censor yet are not asked to.
insights.speaker: Chad (ThorChain co-founder)
insights.so_what: ThorChain's defense rests on equivalence with base layers; the market (and Laura) reject that equivalence, so the defense may not persuade regulators.
insights.quote: They love Bitcoin much more. That's why they use Thorchain to get to Bitcoin.

insights.claim: If enough new validators who want to block laundering joined and reached a two-thirds majority, Chad says laundering would be blocked, since anyone can buy Rune, run a node and vote.
insights.speaker: Chad (ThorChain co-founder)
insights.so_what: Censorship policy is effectively purchasable via bonded Rune; a well-capitalized compliance-minded coalition could change ThorChain's stance.
insights.quote: If you get a two-thirds majority that we should censor transactions, then of course , that’s the community’s choice.

insights.claim: Chad notes that even stolen ThorChain funds could be swapped back through ThorChain itself and the protocol would not have been able to stop it.
insights.speaker: Chad (ThorChain co-founder)
insights.so_what: Underscores the protocol's inability to act fast even in self-interest, a risk factor for LPs in future exploits.

insights.claim: Taylor Monaghan says that for two or three of the past four years co-founder JP had an 'admin key', undermining ThorChain's repeated claims that it could do nothing.
insights.speaker: Taylor Monaghan (security expert)
insights.so_what: Historical existence of privileged keys feeds the 'decentralized in name only' (DINO) narrative and custody/control legal arguments.
insights.quote: for two or three of those four years, we now know that JP had the admin key

insights.claim: Chad says the misnamed 'admin key' could only change configuration (it could not withdraw or redistribute funds, and nodes could undo its changes), and that it was removed from the codebase about a year to a year and a half ago.
insights.speaker: Chad (ThorChain co-founder)
insights.so_what: Removal reduces centralization attack surface but also removes the fastest emergency lever, reinforcing slow responses to illicit flows.
insights.quote: that admin key we're talking about doesn't even exist in the codebase today

insights.claim: In the Thorify incident the admin key was used to suspend the lending function as a temporary stopgap, after which the protocol was updated by two-thirds consensus, which critics cite as proof ThorChain acts quickly when its own interests are threatened.
insights.speaker: Chad (ThorChain co-founder)
insights.so_what: Selective intervention (for self-harm, not external hacks) is the core inconsistency regulators and critics will press on.
insights.quote: The admin key was used to suspend the lending function in that case

insights.claim: ThorChain halted for about five weeks over an issue affecting the protocol itself, unrelated to North Korea.
insights.speaker: Laura Shin (host)
insights.so_what: Shows multi-week halts are acceptable to nodes when their own funds are at stake, weakening the 'halts are too costly' argument.

insights.claim: ThorChain has two governance tiers: operational 'mimirs' need only about three nodes to change configuration (four to roll back, five or six to repeal) for fast vulnerability response, while economic settings require a two-thirds majority; the docs say a supermajority halts the chain while the code says three votes.
insights.speaker: Chad (ThorChain co-founder)
insights.so_what: A handful of nodes can already change operational config quickly, contradicting the claim that any response requires weeks of supermajority consensus.
insights.quote: Operational "mummies" require at least three nodes to make a configuration change

insights.claim: The slashing/ban mechanism (two-thirds of nodes voting to seize a node's bond) has been used once, against an attacker who stole $10 million from ThorChain, around May of this year.
insights.speaker: Chad (ThorChain co-founder)
insights.so_what: Demonstrates that bond confiscation is a live tool, which shapes node-operator risk perception and willingness to dissent.
insights.quote: mathematically proven that an attacker attacked Thor Chain and stole $10 million

insights.claim: Chad offered to propose a community vote to remove the bond-seizure capability for dissent, and said the treasury might consider returning part of the developer-fund share of hack-related fees to victims.
insights.speaker: Chad (ThorChain co-founder)
insights.so_what: Watch for governance proposals on ban-mechanism limits or fee restitution as signals of reputational repair.
insights.quote: I think I will discuss this with the Treasury and talk about this idea.

insights.claim: ThorChain has just over 100 active nodes but only about 50-54 distinct operator addresses, and four operators control 39 nodes, exceeding the one-third threshold that can block signing or consensus.
insights.speaker: Laura Shin (host)
insights.so_what: Effective Nakamoto coefficient of about four means coordination (for censorship or for halts) is easy, which cuts against both the 'can't act' defense and the decentralization narrative.
insights.quote: four operators manage 39 nodes. And this exceeds the 1/3 threshold

insights.claim: Chad argues ThorChain's Nakamoto coefficient of about four beats Bitcoin (three mining pools control 51% of hashpower) and Ethereum (three or four mostly corporate operators like Coinbase and Binance).
insights.speaker: Chad (ThorChain co-founder)
insights.so_what: Decentralization comparisons hinge on which threshold you measure; regulators may weigh custody (TSS vaults) more than raw operator counts.
insights.quote: In Bitcoin, the three mining pools together account for 51% of the computing power.

insights.claim: After the Bybit hack (about $1.4 billion), some validators tried to halt Ethereum trading, lost the vote by a wide margin, and roughly 20 validators left; Chad claims operator and validator counts are now at all-time highs, about 115 including standby.
insights.speaker: Chad (ThorChain co-founder)
insights.so_what: Dissenting, compliance-minded operators self-selected out, so the remaining validator set is structurally less likely to ever vote for censorship.
insights.quote: We actually lost about 20 validators or something

insights.claim: Taylor Monaghan reports that departed node operators told her they feared both social attacks and having their bonded Rune seized by a two-thirds vote if they opposed the majority, which Chad flatly denies was ever discussed.
insights.speaker: Taylor Monaghan (security expert)
insights.so_what: Perceived coercion suppresses governance dissent; a validator set filtered for agreement makes future policy change unlikely.

insights.claim: Chad says operators who left after Bybit did so because they did not support ThorChain being properly decentralized and wanted to avoid problems with regulators, not because they feared bond seizure.
insights.speaker: Chad (ThorChain co-founder)
insights.so_what: Either way, regulatory fear drove operator exits, signalling that sophisticated operators see legal risk in running ThorChain nodes.
insights.quote: they didn't want to have problems with regulators or anything like that

insights.claim: Individual node operators can refuse to observe specific transactions at a cost of a few penalty points that reduce rewards (possibly under a dollar) but never touch their bonded principal.
insights.speaker: Chad (ThorChain co-founder)
insights.so_what: There is a cheap individual opt-out from processing illicit flows; its non-use suggests operators prefer the fee income.
insights.quote: the maximum you can hurt yourself is just lose all the reward but keep the principal

insights.claim: ThorChain's core development is thin: Chad counts five or six core developers and seven or eight people with code-approval rights, while a new core developer said in July there were only three code reviewers.
insights.speaker: Chad (ThorChain co-founder)
insights.so_what: Small reviewer pool is a key-person and security risk for a protocol holding cross-chain vault assets.

themes.theme: Custody, closed-source TSS and legal exposure

insights.claim: OKX's Saru argues ThorChain validators collectively control assets in TSS vaults and can move funds once the signature threshold is reached, so ThorChain is a distributed intermediary rather than a base-layer-like protocol.
insights.speaker: Laura Shin (host)
insights.so_what: Custody framing is exactly what money-transmission law turns on; exchanges like OKX adopting it could lead to delisting or flagging of ThorChain flows.
insights.quote: distributing the middleman does not eliminate the middleman itself

insights.claim: ThorChain's TSS signing library was made closed source after an exploit a few months ago so the security team could analyze it; Chad says it will be reopened but gives no date, and it ships via Docker images.
insights.speaker: Chad (ThorChain co-founder)
insights.so_what: Nodes run unverifiable signing code, a security and decentralization red flag until source is republished; watch for the reopen.
insights.quote: It was made private recently due to an exploit that happened a few months ago

insights.claim: Laura Shin argues ThorChain may fare worse than Tornado Cash under DOJ's custody-and-control test, citing a 2025 speech by Acting Assistant Attorney General Galiotti that Section 1960 unlicensed money-transmission charges don't apply only where no third party has custody and control of user assets.
insights.speaker: Laura Shin (host)
insights.so_what: Operator co-custody of vaults is the legal pressure point; enforcement action against node operators or contributors is a tail risk for Rune.
insights.quote: where a third party does not have custody and control over the users' assets, then, um, these charges under Section 1960 do not apply

insights.claim: Chad says lawyers have expressed little concern and that in 2022 or 2023 US three-letter agencies approached him, wanting to understand ThorChain including its administrators, but showed little interest and were not hostile.
insights.speaker: Chad (ThorChain co-founder)
insights.so_what: Management's low perceived legal risk predates the 2025 DOJ guidance and the latest hacks, so it may be stale.
insights.quote: A few years ago I spoke to the US government agencies that have three- letter acronyms.

insights.claim: The swap.thorchain.org interface, controlled by the treasury rather than the protocol, filters hacker addresses, which Chad frames as a normal centralized front-end that follows the law.
insights.speaker: Chad (ThorChain co-founder)
insights.so_what: Compliance happens only at the UI layer; launderers bypass it by hitting the protocol directly, so front-end filtering does little to stop flows.
insights.quote: the user interface is controlled by the treasury. It is not controlled by the protocol.

insights.claim: TRM encourages exchanges to scrutinize bitcoin coming out of ThorChain vaults, especially after hacks; Chad says ThorChain has processed about $125 billion over the past few years, of which maybe 1-2% is illicit.
insights.speaker: Chad (ThorChain co-founder)
insights.so_what: Analytics-firm risk flags on ThorChain outputs can raise friction for legitimate users at exchanges, a demand headwind for the protocol.
insights.quote: we’ve transacted about $125 billion in transactions over the past few years . Maybe 1% or 2% of that is illicit funds

insights.claim: An undercover investigation by Zach XBT exposed a Chinese crime syndicate that laundered $1.5 billion of Bybit funds, whose member recommended ThorChain cross-chain for laundering, and the contact was met via the ThorChain Discord.
insights.speaker: Laura Shin (host)
insights.so_what: ThorChain being named in launderer playbooks increases sanctions/enforcement headline risk.
insights.quote: All you need is Thor crosschain.

insights.claim: Near Intents' risk shield can reject quotes or halt swaps mid-execution; it blocked a $50 million laundering attempt, froze about half a million and plans to return $340,000, while ThorChain says such a feature would be up to validators and is unlikely.
insights.speaker: Laura Shin (host)
insights.so_what: Competing cross-chain swap venues are differentiating on compliance tooling, which may win institutional and exchange flow from ThorChain.
insights.quote: they tweeted that permissionless doesn't mean neutral

insights.claim: ThorChain protocol fees showed two huge spikes in recent months, each following a major hack, and in one week about $1.3 billion of volume generated an estimated $12 million in fees, described as conservative.
insights.speaker: Taylor Monaghan (security expert)
insights.so_what: Hack-driven volume inflates ThorChain revenue metrics; treat fee spikes after hacks as non-recurring and reputationally toxic when valuing Rune.
insights.quote: It was 1.3 billion in volume in a week and 10 million in commissions

insights.claim: Chad argues illicit-fee revenue is barely noticeable over the protocol's full history and compares it to Uniswap also earning fees on North Korean transactions.
insights.speaker: Chad (ThorChain co-founder)
insights.so_what: Long-run averages hide that in short windows illicit flow is the majority of volume and fees, so revenue is lumpy and event-dependent.
insights.quote: if you look at the entire time span of the protocol's history, it's barely noticeable

insights.claim: The ThorChain developer fund receives about 5% of the fee waterfall, and Chad said he had not checked how much it has received in a long time.
insights.speaker: Chad (ThorChain co-founder)
insights.so_what: Most fee value flows to nodes and LPs, concentrating the incentive problem with node operators who decide on halts.
insights.quote: The developer fund receives about 5%, which is a very small share.

insights.claim: Taylor Monaghan argues the core incentive problem is that ThorChain participants profit directly from stolen-fund volume, making them less inclined to act, and that even six-figure restitution would signal they do not want to profit.
insights.speaker: Taylor Monaghan (security expert)
insights.so_what: Incentive misalignment means policy change is unlikely without external (regulatory/exchange) pressure.
